be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

The orthogonal operators on a finite-dimensional real inner product space form a group under composition, as do the unitary operators on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space. Every such operator $T$ satisfies

$$|\det T|=1.$$

Over $\mathbb R$, this says $\det T\in\{-1,1\}$. In dimension zero, the unique determinant is $1$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

A **smooth $n$-manifold** is a pair $(M,\mathcal S)$ in which $M$ is a
topological $n$-manifold
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]) and $\mathcal S$ is a **smooth
structure** on $M$: a maximal smooth atlas
([[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]]).
Because
[[thm-each-smooth-atlas-is-contained-in-a-unique-maximal-smooth-atlas]] sends
every smooth atlas to the unique maximal atlas containing it, a smooth manifold
is equivalently specified by a topological manifold $M$ together with any one
smooth atlas $\mathcal A$, the structure being the generated $[\mathcal A]$. A
chart $(U,\varphi)\in\mathcal S$ is called a **smooth chart** (or a **chart of
the smooth structure**); its domain is a **coordinate domain** and its
coordinate functions are **smooth coordinates** on $U$. When the structure is
clear from context, the manifold itself is written $M$ in place of
$(M,\mathcal S)$.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. The compatibility of these local formulas is proved in [[lem-the-riemannian-volume-density-is-coordinate-independent]].
The local Riemannian volume densities glue to a positive smooth density independent of coordinates.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If $r$ is a finite-valued positive smooth density, $\mu_r$ is finite on compact sets, locally finite, sigma-finite, and a regular Borel measure, hence Radon. Its completion is denoted $(M,\overline{\mathcal B(M)},\overline\mu_r)$ and is not identified with its Borel domain.

Under countable choice, the density $\mu_g$ defines a compact-finite, locally finite, sigma-finite Radon Borel measure $\operatorname{vol}_g$. Its completion has a separately specified completed domain. Smooth compact-support integrals agree with smooth density integration, and finite-radius metric balls are Borel.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: A skew-Hermitian matrix has purely imaginary diagonal entries, giving $N$ real parameters. For each $i<j$, its $(i,j)$ entry is an arbitrary complex number and the $(j,i)$ entry is then forced to be its negative conjugate, giving two real parameters. Thus $\mathfrak u(N)$ has real dimension $N+2\binom N2=N^2$.

If $(I-X)v=0$ for $X^*=-X$, then $Xv=v$. But $v^*Xv$ is purely imaginary because $X^*=-X$, while this equality gives $v^*Xv=v^*v>0$ for nonzero $v$. Hence $I-X$ is invertible. Direct multiplication, using that $I-X$ and $I+X$ commute, shows $(I+X)(I-X)^{-1}$ is unitary.

On the open set of unitary matrices $Q$ near $I$ where $Q+I$ is invertible, the inverse formula is $X=(Q-I)(Q+I)^{-1}$. The factors are polynomials in $Q$, so they commute; using $Q^*=Q^{-1}$ gives $X^*=-X$. The forward and inverse formulas are smooth rational matrix maps, and therefore define a chart of dimension $N^2$ near $I$.

Left translation by any fixed $Q_0\in U(N)$ sends a Cayley neighborhood of $I$ to a chart neighborhood of $Q_0$, so these translates cover $U(N)$. The group is closed, since $Q^*Q=I$ is a closed matrix equation, and bounded, since every column has norm one. Identifying $M_N(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^{2N^2}$, [F1] makes $U(N)$ compact. Its subspace topology is Hausdorff and second-countable: the Euclidean metric restricts to a separating metric, and intersections with rational Euclidean balls form a countable base. On overlaps, translated Cayley transition maps are compositions of the forward and inverse rational formulas from step 3.1 with fixed matrix multiplication; matrix inversion is smooth on its open domain, so the transitions are smooth. Thus a finite subcover of these neighborhoods is a finite smooth atlas on a topological $N^2$-manifold, and [F2] supplies its smooth structure.

The Frobenius inner product is left invariant because $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}((Q_0A)^*Q_0B)=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$. By [F3] it defines a Riemannian metric; [F4] and [F5] give its global positive smooth volume density. In each of the finitely many charts from step 4.1, take all rational coordinate balls whose closed balls lie in the chart domain. These balls form a countable cover without making pointwise choices. Compactness gives a finite subcover. On each selected closed ball the smooth density coefficient is bounded, so its integral is finite; every nonempty coordinate ball has positive integral. The total smooth volume is therefore finite and positive, so it can be normalized.

Under [A1], [F6] and [F7] make the associated Borel measure a regular left-invariant Radon measure; the normalization from step 5.1 makes it a probability. In each chart the density coefficient is smooth and strictly positive, so a Borel set is $\mu_F$-null exactly when its coordinate image is Lebesgue-null.

Under [A2], this normalized left-invariant probability on the compact group agrees with normalized Haar probability by uniqueness in [F8]. This proves only the optional Haar branch; the volume-null statement was proved in step 6.1.

product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: Apply [F1] to $A$ to obtain unitary $L_0,R_0$ and $C_0=\operatorname{diag}(c_1,\dots,c_k)$ with $A=L_0C_0R_0^*$ and $c_i\ge0$. Since $A$ is the compression of the unitary $U$ to the first block, $\|Av\|\le\|v\|$ for every $v$, so each singular value satisfies $c_i\le1$. Put $S_0=\operatorname{diag}(s_i)$ with $s_i=\sqrt{1-c_i^2}$.

The first block row of $UU^*=I$ gives $AA^*+BB^*=I$, hence $(L_0^*B)(L_0^*B)^*=S_0^2$. For every $i$ with $s_i>0$, the row $s_i^{-1}e_i^*L_0^*B$ has norm one, and these rows are mutually orthogonal by the displayed Gram identity. Extend them to an orthonormal basis using [F3], and choose the signs of the completed rows so that a unitary $W$ satisfies $L_0^*B=-S_0W^*$.

The first block column of $U^*U=I$ gives $A^*A+C^*C=I$, hence $(CR_0)^*(CR_0)=S_0^2$. For every $i$ with $s_i>0$, the column $s_i^{-1}CR_0e_i$ has norm one, and these columns are mutually orthogonal. Extend them to an orthonormal basis using [F3]; the resulting unitary $Z$ satisfies $CR_0=ZS_0$. Therefore $\widetilde U:=\operatorname{diag}(L_0^*,Z^*)U\operatorname{diag}(R_0,W)=\begin{pmatrix}C_0&-S_0\\S_0&E\end{pmatrix}$ for some $E$.

The upper-right block of $\widetilde U\widetilde U^*=I$ gives $S_0E^*=C_0S_0$. Thus, for each $i$ with $s_i>0$, column $i$ of $E$ is $c_ie_i$. The lower-right blocks of $\widetilde U\widetilde U^*=I$ and $\widetilde U^*\widetilde U=I$ give $EE^*=E^*E=C_0^2$. For such $i$, the prescribed entry $E_{ii}=c_i$ already contributes $c_i^2$ to row $i$'s squared norm, so $EE^*=C_0^2$ forces every other entry in that row to vanish. Thus both the rows and columns indexed by $P=\{i:s_i>0\}$ have no cross-block entries. On $K=\{i:s_i=0\}$ one has $c_i=1$; the $K\times K$ block of $E$ has orthonormal rows and columns and is therefore unitary. This also covers $c_i=0$, where the corresponding row and column are zero, and $c_i=1$, where the index belongs to $K$.

Let $Q$ be that unitary $K\times K$ block and replace $Z$ by $Z'=Z\operatorname{diag}(I,Q)$. Since $Q$ acts only where $S_0=0$ and $C_0=I$, this leaves $CR_0=Z'S_0$ unchanged and changes the lower-right block to $C_0$. Hence $U=\operatorname{diag}(L_0,Z')\begin{pmatrix}C_0&-S_0\\S_0&C_0\end{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(R_0^*,W^*).$ Both outside factors are unitary, and $C_0^2+S_0^2=I$ by definition. The argument includes $c_i=0$, $c_i=1$, repeated values, and empty positive or zero supports.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge1$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$. Its **determinant** is
$$\det(A):=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_{i<n}a_{\sigma(i),i}.$$
The sum is finite because $S_n$ has $n!$ elements. The product is taken in $R$, so the signs $1$ and $-1$ act through the ring identities. The formula uses columns indexed by $i<n$ and rows indexed by $\sigma(i)$.

When $A$ is real, $|\det A|$ means the ordinary real absolute value of its real determinant. It is not alternate notation for the determinant itself.

$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

The matrix $S=\widehat W^T\widehat W$ is symmetric; since $S^*=\overline S$ and $\widehat W$ is unitary, $S^*S=I$, so $S$ is unitary.

Direct calculation from the definition of $S$ gives $S^T=S$ and $S^*S=I$. Write $S=P+iR$ with $P,R$ real symmetric. From $S\overline S=I$ we obtain $P^2+R^2=I$ and $PR=RP$. Apply [F2] first to $P$. The restriction $R|_{E_\lambda}$ is self-adjoint for the inherited inner product, since $\langle Ru,v\rangle=\langle u,Rv\rangle$. By [F6]–[F7] and $\det\widehat W=1$, $\det S=\det(\widehat W^T)\det(\widehat W)=1$, so $\prod_jd_j$ is either $1$ or $-1$; if it is $-1$, change the sign of one root. Put $R_0=\widehat W K^{-1}$. It is unitary and $R_0^TR_0=K^{-1}\widehat W^T\widehat W K^{-1}=K^{-1}SK^{-1}=I.$ Thus $R_0^T=R_0^*$, which entrywise says $R_0$ is real. Also $\det R_0=1$, so $R_0\in SO(4)$, and $\widehat W=R_0OD_0O^T$.

Input: an exact-arithmetic representation of $U\in U(N)$, $N\ge1$, supporting addition, multiplication, conjugation, nonnegative square roots, exact zero tests, and exact division by nonzero positive real scalars. Output: a finite ordered factorization into two-level unitaries and a diagonal unitary. This is an exact algebraic procedure; no claim of a bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real input is made.

Initialize $M:=U$ and an empty chronological list. For each column $j=0,\ldots,N-2$, and for $r=N-1,N-2,\ldots,j+1$, set $a=M_{r-1,j}$ and $b=M_{r,j}$. If $b=0$, do nothing. Otherwise set $h=\sqrt{|a|^2+|b|^2}>0$ and left-multiply rows $(r-1,r)$ by
$$G=\frac1h\begin{pmatrix}\overline a&\overline b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix},$$
recording this two-level unitary in the order applied. Let the resulting matrix be $D$. Return the factorization $U=G_1^*\cdots G_s^*D$. In chronological circuit order, apply $D$ first and then $G_s^*,\ldots,G_1^*$.

derivations.claim: If $b\ne0$, then $h>0$ and direct multiplication gives $G^*G=I_2$ and $G(a,b)^T=(h,0)^T$. Thus the row operation is defined and left multiplication by its coordinate embedding preserves unitarity of $M$. If $b=0$, skipping the operation leaves the desired entry zero.

Inductively, before processing column $j$, columns $0,\ldots,j-1$ have zero entries below their diagonal positions. Each row pair used for column $j$ has indices at least $j$, so both entries in every earlier column are zero and the row operation preserves those zeros. Descending $r$ therefore makes column $j$ zero below its diagonal without undoing a zero already made in that column.

After the finite loops, $D=G_s\cdots G_1U$ is upper triangular and unitary. Its first column has only its first entry nonzero, which has modulus one. Orthogonality with every later column forces the first entry of each later column to be zero. Removing the first row and column leaves an upper-triangular unitary block; induction proves that $D$ is diagonal with unit-modulus diagonal entries.

Rearranging $D=G_s\cdots G_1U$ gives $U=G_1^*\cdots G_s^*D$ exactly. The finite loops have $\sum_{j=0}^{N-2}(N-j-1)=N(N-1)/2$ iterations (zero for $N=1$), with at most one row elimination per iteration, so they terminate with at most that many eliminations and at most $N$ diagonal phases; the zero tests skip any already-zero entry. Under the convention that a matrix product acts on column states from right to left, the same identity orders the actions as $D$ first and then $G_s^*,\ldots,G_1^*$.

$$ r>\max\{m-n,0\}. $$

Then the critical value set of $f$ is a null subset of $\mathbb R^n$.

For $N\ge1$, define $U(N)=\{Q\in M_N(\mathbb C):Q^*Q=QQ^*=I\}$ and $\mathfrak u(N)=\{X\in M_N(\mathbb C):X^*=-X\}$, both regarded as real spaces where appropriate. Then $U(N)$ is a compact smooth real manifold of dimension $N^2$. Near $I$, the Cayley map
$$X\longmapsto (I+X)(I-X)^{-1}$$
is a smooth chart from $\mathfrak u(N)$; left translates give a finite atlas. The Frobenius inner product induces a smooth Riemannian metric. Under AC$_\omega$, its volume density defines a normalized Borel volume probability $\mu_F$; a Borel subset is $\mu_F$-null exactly when its intersection with every chart has Lebesgue-null coordinate image. Under AC, $\mu_F$ is the normalized Haar probability, so this also gives the Haar-null criterion in that branch.

In the ordered computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$ of [[def-qc-qubit-and-bloch-representation]], define the identity and Pauli endomorphisms of $Q_2$ by

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

derivations.claim: A matrix in $SU(2)$ has the form $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\-\bar b&\bar a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$: its first column is a unit vector, orthogonality and determinant one fix the second column, as in the two-column calculation in the Euler proof. Conversely, direct multiplication verifies that every displayed matrix is unitary with determinant one. Thus $SU(2)$ is $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. On each of the eight open sets where one real coordinate is positive or negative, solve that coordinate as $\pm\sqrt{1-u_1^2-u_2^2-u_3^2}$; these smooth charts show $SU(2)$ is a real 3-manifold. It is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F7]. The tangent Lie algebra is the three-dimensional span in [F6]. Thus $G=SU(2)^n$ is a compact smooth real manifold of dimension $3n$. Collecting consecutive one-qubit gates into local layers and moving every scalar factor to the front writes each circuit with the fixed skeleton as $e^{i\phi}K_mC_mK_{m-1}\cdots C_1K_0,$ where $K_j\in G$. The scalar phases commute with all gates and combine into one real parameter $\phi$; [F1] parameterizes each one-qubit special-unitary factor by three real angles. The chronological matrix convention is [F8], and [F9] fixes the counted gate alphabet.

Direct inspection of the matrices in [F6] shows that every traceless skew-Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix is a unique real combination of $iX,iY,iZ$: its diagonal entries are $ir,-ir$ and its off-diagonal entries are $z,-\bar z$, with $r\in\mathbb R,z\in\mathbb C$. Fix one CNOT $C_j$ with control $c$ and target $t$. Applying its basis action [F2] to the four affected basis vectors gives $C_jZ_cC_j=Z_c$ and $C_jX_tC_j=X_t$. By [F10], the CNOT basis permutation is unitary. Its local commuting subgroup $H_j\le G$ therefore consists of arbitrary $SU(2)$ factors on the $n-2$ other wires, rotations $e^{isZ}$ on $c$, and rotations $e^{irX}$ on $t$. This product has real dimension $3(n-2)+1+1=3n-4$. A complementary subspace $\mathfrak m_j$ of $\mathfrak{su}(2)^n$ is spanned by $iX_c,iY_c,iY_t,iZ_t$ and has dimension four.

Give $\mathfrak m_j\times H_j$ and $G$ local coordinates from the $S^3$ charts in step 1.1 and angle charts on the two circles in $H_j$. The local product map $\Phi_j:\mathfrak m_j\times H_j\to G$, $(X,h)\mapsto e^Xh$, has derivative at $(0,I)$ equal to $(X,Y)\mapsto X+Y$. The direct sum $\mathfrak m_j\oplus\mathfrak h_j=\mathfrak{su}(2)^n$ makes this derivative an isomorphism between $3n$-dimensional coordinate spaces, so [F3] gives neighborhoods on which every nearby local factor is $e^Xh$ with four real coordinates in $X$ and $h\in H_j$. The group $G$ is compact: each $SU(2)$ is the closed bounded set of matrices $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\-\bar b&\bar a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with $|a|^2+|b|^2=1$, and a finite product of compact sets is compact. Translating the neighborhood and using compactness gives a finite cover of $G$ by such local product charts.

Starting with $K_m$ and proceeding downwards, use a finite chart to write the current local factor as $g_\ell e^{X_j}h_j$, where $g_\ell$ is one of finitely many fixed local translations and $X_j$ has four real coordinates. Since $h_j$ commutes with $C_j$, move it through $C_j$ and multiply it into the next local factor; that product remains in $G$. Repeating this for all $m$ CNOTs leaves $m$ four-parameter factors and one arbitrary local layer $K_0$ with $3n$ parameters. Each chart choice has finitely many possibilities, and the global phase adds one parameter, so the exact image is contained in a finite union of smooth images with dimension $4m+3n+1$.

The exact circuit set is compact, hence Borel: by step 1.1 it is the continuous image of the compact space $S^1\times G^{m+1}$. Each open Euclidean parameter domain has a countable compact exhaustion, so each smooth parameter image is a countable union of compact, hence closed, subsets of $U(2^n)$ and is Borel. If $4m+3n+1<4^n$, every point of each parameter domain is critical for the smooth map into a target chart of $U(2^n)$, since its derivative has rank at most the smaller domain dimension. A finite union over parameter-chart choices is still null. Under full AC, [F5] identifies that null set as Haar-null. Thus the fixed skeleton has the claimed null image.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

For square matrices $U,V$ of the same size, write $U\sim_{\mathrm{phase}}V$ when $U=\lambda V$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ with $|\lambda|=1$. This relation is kept distinct from exact matrix equality.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space; the pairing is linear in its first argument ([[def-dimension]], [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Write $\mathcal L(H)$ for its complex-linear endomorphisms ([[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]]) and let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty outcome set. A **finite POVM** on $H$ with outcomes $\Omega$ is a family $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ with each $E_a$ nonnegative and $\sum_{a\in\Omega}E_a=I_H$; after any enumeration of $\Omega$, these operators form the finite complete positive family of [[def-qc-finite-positive-effect-family]]. Reordering does not alter the finite sum. The complete-family lemma [[lem-qc-complete-effect-family-members-are-effects]] shows that every $E_a$ also has nonnegative complement $I_H-E_a$, so each is an effect.

For a density operator $\rho$ on $H$ (a nonnegative operator of trace one, [[def-qc-density-operator]]), its **POVM outcome weights** are

$$p_\rho(a):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a),\qquad a\in\Omega.$$

Here $\operatorname{tr}$ is the finite-dimensional endomorphism trace ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

The positivity and normalization of these weights are proved in [[thm-qc-povm-probabilities-normalize]]. A POVM specifies this outcome law; it does not by itself prescribe a conditional output state.

Let $\rho$ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $H$, and let $E=(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ be a finite POVM on $H$. Then

$$p_\rho(a)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)\in[0,1]\quad\text{for each }a\in\Omega,\qquad \sum_{a\in\Omega}p_\rho(a)=1.$$

derivations.claim: The diagonal blocks of $C(\lambda U)$ are $I_H$ and $\lambda U$. Multiplying the blocks of $(P_\lambda\otimes I_H)C(U)$ gives $I_H$ and $\lambda U$, so the two full matrices are equal exactly.

Under the whole-output update specified in the Given, $(\lambda I)\rho(\lambda I)^*=\lambda\overline\lambda\rho=\rho$ because $|\lambda|=1$. Hence the whole-output scalar leaves the density operator unchanged.

By [F2], $U$ and $\lambda U$ are phase-equivalent as target matrices. If $\lambda\ne1$, $P_\lambda$ is not a scalar multiple of the identity: its diagonal entries are $1$ and $\lambda$. Thus step 1.1 places a phase on only the active control block. Left multiplication by $P_{\overline\lambda}\otimes I_H$ changes the blocks back to $I_H,U$, so it restores $C(U)$ exactly. For $\lambda=1$ no correction is needed.

By [F4], each defined measurement weight is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_a)$. The equality of density operators in step 1.2 makes these weights identical for every outcome $a$. Under the normalized-law conclusion [F5], the two probability distributions therefore agree. The global scalar in step 1.2 preserves the whole measurement law, while the controlled target scalar in step 1.1 does not become a whole-output scalar.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $U_0,U_1$ be unitary endomorphisms of $H$. On the control-first direct sum $H\oplus H$, the block unitary $\operatorname{diag}(U_0,U_1)$ factors as

$$M=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle\langle x|\otimes R_a(\theta_x),\qquad R_a(t)=\exp(-it\sigma_a/2).$$

Every $U\in U(4)$ has an exact circuit with no ancillas, at most three CNOT gates, and arbitrary one-qubit gates. The scalar phase is implemented as a one-qubit scalar gate and is not discarded.

For the central multiplexed $R_y$, use the Gray traversal of [F3] with controlled-$Z$ in place of CNOT. Take the last Gray edge as a terminal controlled-$Z$ and absorb it into the neighboring generic block-diagonal factor before demultiplexing that factor. In its first-wire control blocks it multiplies the lower-register branch by $I$ or by the single-wire $Z$ on its select wire. Both branches remain arbitrary unitaries, so [F2] still gives four recursive children and two multiplexed $R_z$ factors. The full block identity is $LMR=(LE_r)TR=\operatorname{diag}(L_0,L_1Z_r)TR$ by [F10], where $M=E_rT$ and $T$ omits the terminal controlled-$Z$. Each recursive call removes the first wire of its contiguous interval, so all $N=4^{n-2}$ terminal slots act on the same last two wires. Every nonterminal multiplexed rotation targets a wire strictly before these two. Its select operations preserve the computational labels of the last two wires: branch by branch in those labels, its rotations and controlled-$X$ or controlled-$Z$ gates act on other wires. Products of these separator operations therefore have exactly the block form required by [A1]. The preceding controlled-$Z$ absorption only changes the arbitrary child matrices before their recursive decomposition and does not change this target/select invariant. citations.quote: Assume AC$_\omega$ to form normalized Frobenius volume on $U(2^n)$. For fixed $n\ge1$ and a fixed ordered CNOT skeleton with $m$ CNOTs, arbitrary exact one-qubit gates, and no ancillas, the set of exact circuit matrices is contained in a finite union of smooth images of real parameter spaces of dimension at most $3n+4m+1$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. For every sequence
$(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets there is a sequence
$(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ with $a_n\in A_n$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$. Thus the
Axiom of Choice implies the pair-local countable choice principle
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]).

derivations.claim: By [F2], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $U$. For a unit eigenvector $v$ of eigenvalue $\lambda$, $1=\|Uv\|=|\lambda|$, so [F3] writes $\lambda=\cos t+i\sin t$. Set $\mu=\cos(t/2)+i\sin(t/2)$. The double-angle identities give $\mu^2=\lambda$, and hence $|\mu|^2=|\lambda|=1$. Putting these unit-modulus roots on the diagonal in that eigenbasis and conjugating back gives a unitary $V$ with $V^2=U$.

For the clean-bit branch, let $w$ start at $0$. An $m$-controlled $X$ into $w$, using the data target as the returned borrowed wire, changes $w$ to the AND of the controls. Apply $C(U)$ controlled by $w$ and reverse the same $X$ circuit. On each computational-basis input this applies $U$ exactly on the all-one control branch by [F5] and restores $w=0$ by [F4]; linearity gives the same exact operator on superpositions. The two $X$ calls and one controlled-$U$ call cost $O(m)$ in the model [F6] by [A1].

For the lower bound, make an undirected graph with one vertex for every circuit wire, including controls, target, and any workspace, and one edge for each two-qubit gate joining its two wires. If some control were disconnected from the target, the full circuit factors across the graph components. Choose the same data-independent auxiliary state for both test inputs (for the dirty contract a fixed product state is permitted). Even if that auxiliary state has correlations between components, a unitary on the disconnected component cannot change the reduced state of the target component: taking the partial trace cancels that unitary with its adjoint. The target reduced state would therefore be unchanged when that control alone is toggled. Since nonscalar unitary $U$ has two orthogonal eigenvectors $u,v$ with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda,\mu$, the state $\psi=(u+v)/\sqrt2$ obeys $U\psi=(\lambda u+\mu v)/\sqrt2$, which is not a scalar multiple of $\psi$. Set all other controls to $1$ and the target to $\psi$; toggling the disconnected control changes the required target ray from $[\psi]$ to $[U\psi]$, a contradiction. Thus the target component contains all $m$ controls and has at least $m+1$ vertices. A connected component on at least $m+1$ vertices has at least $m$ edges, so at least $m$ two-qubit gates are needed.

For $m\ge2$, write $A$ for the AND of the first $m-1$ control bits and $b$ for the last control. In chronological order [F7], the recursive controlled-$V$ construction applies $V$ to the target under $b$, toggles $b$ by an $(m-1)$-controlled $X$ under the first controls, applies $V^*$ under the changed $b$, toggles $b$ back, then applies $V$ under the first controls. On a basis branch the exponent of $V$ on the target is $b-(b\oplus A)+A$: it is $0$ when $A=0$, $0$ when $(A,b)=(1,0)$, and $2$ when $(A,b)=(1,1)$. Thus the ideal branch matrices are $I,I,V^2=U$, exactly the required $C^m(U)$ action by [F5]. Implementing the two controlled-$X$ calls with the data target as borrowed wire, and the final recursive controlled-$V$ call with the restored $b$ as borrowed wire, yields $q_m\le q_{m-1}+2x_{m-1}+O(1)$, where $x_r$ is the borrowed-bit controlled-$X$ cost. By [F8]–[F9], $x_1=1$; [A1] gives $x_r=O(r)$ for $r\ge2$, so summing the recurrence from the constant one-control base [F1] gives $q_m=O(m^2)$ in the gate model [F6]. Every borrowed-wire call is the required controlled operation tensored with identity, so using the data target as its borrowed wire is valid even when it is entangled with the controls. The recursive call uses only its own controls and target; the restored $b$ is available but is not needed as an extra wire.

The lower bound is linear and the no-work upper bound is quadratic, so no quadratic optimality claim follows. The no-workspace recursion and clean-bit compute/apply/uncompute construction prove the two upper bounds, with exact work-bit return supplied by [A1].

citations.quote: Let a finite ordered register have an orthonormal computational basis $(|z\rangle)_{z\in\mathcal X}$, using the root convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. For distinct labels $x,y\in\mathcal X$, choose $V\in U(2)$, where $U(2)=\{M\in M_2(\mathbb C):M^*M=MM^*=I_2\}$. The **two-level unitary** $T_{x,y}(V)$ acts by the matrix $V$ in the ordered basis $(|x\rangle,|y\rangle)$ and acts as the identity on $\operatorname{span}\{|x\rangle,|y\rangle\}^{\perp}$. Its action is exact matrix equality: any scalar phase contained in $V$ is retained.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$ with maximum arity $k:=\max(\{r(g):g\in G\}\cup\{0\})$ and a circuit from [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The declared **size** is the number of gate occurrences, equivalently $\sum_{t=1}^d|L_t|$; the declared **depth** is the number $d$ of explicit layers, not a minimum over alternate layerings; the **width** is the number $n$ of all wires, including workspace wires. The operation model may also assign weighted gate costs, classical bit costs, and query costs; these are separate coordinates and are summed over the calls actually made.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

For $m\ge1$ controls and exact $U\in U(2)$, define
$$C^m(U)=\sum_{x\ne1^m}|x\rangle\langle x|\otimes I_2+|1^m\rangle\langle1^m|\otimes U.$$
This controlled operation has (i) a no-workspace exact construction with $O(m^2)$ one-qubit and CNOT gates, and (ii) an exact construction using one clean work bit, initially $0$ and returned to $0$, with $O(m)$ such gates. For nonscalar $U$, every exact circuit needs at least $m$ two-qubit gates, also when auxiliary wires are allowed with data-independent initial state and exact clean or dirty return. Clean auxiliary wires start at $0$ and return to $0$ for every data input; dirty auxiliary wires may start in any state and the full operation is $C^m(U)\otimes I$ on them, including correlated inputs. A fixed auxiliary state may be internally entangled but is initially independent of the data. These are upper/lower bounds; the quadratic no-work construction is not asserted optimal.

For every integer $r\ge1$, an $r$-controlled $X$ on $r$ control wires and one target has an exact circuit of $O(r)$ arbitrary one-qubit gates and CNOTs when one additional borrowed wire is available. The circuit equals $C^r(X)\otimes I$ on the entire register: the borrowed wire is returned unchanged for every state, including states entangled with the controls, target, or an external register. No wire is initialized or measured.

For every $U\in U(2)$, the exact controlled matrix $C(U)=\operatorname{diag}(I_2,U)$ is realized with two CNOTs and one-qubit gates only. The scalar phase of $U$ is implemented as a phase gate on the control and is not discarded.

Input distinct $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$, $n\ge1$, exact $V\in U(2)$, and for each controlled call a choice between the no-workspace and clean-bit constructions of [[thm-qc-multicontrolled-ancilla-resource-tradeoff]]. If any call selects the clean-bit construction, supply one clean bit initialized to $0$. Output: the chronological elementary-gate list on the $n$ data wires and, if selected, that one clean work wire.

Let $g_0=x,\ldots,g_d=y$ be the path that flips the differing bit positions once in increasing order, where $d$ is the Hamming distance. For $j=0,\ldots,d-2$, swap $g_j$ and $g_{j+1}$ by an $X$ on their differing bit controlled on the other $n-1$ bits matching their common pattern. Apply $V$ to the final pair $g_{d-1},y$ by a one-qubit target gate controlled on their common other bits, reversing the ordered $2\times2$ block if $g_{d-1}$ has target bit $1$. Undo the swaps in reverse order. Expand every multi-control using its selected construction; implement negative controls by conjugating that control wire with $X$.

Expand the calls by the following procedures. Every list below is chronological; concatenation means execute the left list first. Order control wires and available spare wires by their register positions. All parameter selections are exact mathematical operations: use exact matrix arithmetic, a finite-dimensional unitary eigendecomposition, polar arguments and the Euler parameter selection of [[thm-qc-one-qubit-euler-decomposition]]. The input representation must support these selections and exact zero tests; no finite-precision bit-time claim is made. Fix each selection when its call is first expanded and retain the resulting list for an inverse call.

For one control $c$, target $t$ and matrix $W$, choose $W=e^{i\delta}R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta)$ as in [[thm-qc-one-qubit-euler-decomposition]]. Form the three matrices $A=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta/2)$, $B=R_y(-\theta/2)R_z(- (\alpha+\beta)/2)$ and $C=R_z((\beta-\alpha)/2)$. Define $S(c,t;W)$ to be the list $C_t$, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{c\to t}$, $B_t$, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{c\to t}$, $A_t$, $\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\delta})_c$. Each of $A,B,C$ is one arbitrary one-qubit gate, as in [[thm-qc-one-control-unitary-two-cnot]]. Define $T(a,b;t)$ by setting $J=((1+i)I+(1-i)X)/2$ and concatenating $S(b,t;J)$, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{a\to b}$, $S(b,t;J^*)$, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{a\to b}$, $S(a,t;J)$.

Define the ladder list $L(c_1,\ldots,c_s;t)$ with an ordered supply of at least $\max\{s-2,0\}$ distinct spare wires. For $s=1$ emit one CNOT; for $s=2$ emit $T(c_1,c_2;t)$. For $s\ge3$, use the first $s-2$ spares $a_1,\ldots,a_{s-2}$. Set $T_1=T(c_1,c_2;a_1)$, $T_j=T(c_{j+1},a_{j-1};a_j)$ for $2\le j\le s-2$, and $H=T(c_s,a_{s-2};t)$. Concatenate $T_1,\ldots,T_{s-2},H,T_{s-2},\ldots,T_1$ and then $T_2,\ldots,T_{s-2},H,T_{s-2},\ldots,T_2$; the latter list is just $H$ when $s=3$. This is the borrowed ladder used in [[lem-qc-borrowed-bit-multicontrolled-x-linear]].

Define $D(C;t;z)$ for an ordered nonempty control set $C$ and a distinct borrowed wire $z$. With one or two controls use the corresponding ladder base case and leave $z$ unused. With $r\ge3$ controls split $C$ into its first $p=\lceil r/2\rceil$ controls $A$ and the remaining $q=\lfloor r/2\rfloor$ controls $B$. Let $F=L(A;z)$ use spares from $B\cup\{t\}$, and let $G=L(B\cup\{z\};t)$ use spares from $A$. Emit $F,G,F,G$, using the same parameter choices for repeated lists. The stated spare supplies have at least $p-2$ and $q-1$ wires, respectively.

Define the positive-control no-workspace expansion $N(C;t;W)$ recursively. If $C$ is empty, emit $W_t$. If it has one wire $c$, emit $S(c,t;W)$. Otherwise write $C=A\cup\{b\}$, with $b$ its last control. Choose an orthonormal eigendecomposition $W=R\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)R^*$ by [[thm-complex-spectral-theorem-for-normal-endomorphisms]], choose polar angles $\lambda_j=\cos u_j+i\sin u_j$ by [[thm-polar-form-with-unique-principal-argument]], and set $Z=R\operatorname{diag}(\cos(u_1/2)+i\sin(u_1/2),\cos(u_2/2)+i\sin(u_2/2))R^*$. The addition formulas of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] specify these half-angle roots. Emit $S(b,t;Z)$, $D(A;b;t)$, $S(b,t;Z^*)$, $D(A;b;t)$, $N(A;t;Z)$. The last call has one fewer control and uses only its indicated wires.

For the positive-control clean-bit expansion with nonempty $C$ and clean wire $w$, emit $D(C;w;t)$, $S(w,t;W)$, and the reversed adjoint of that same $D$ list. With no controls emit $W_t$ and leave $w$ unused. These are the two constructions analyzed in [[thm-qc-multicontrolled-ancilla-resource-tradeoff]]. For a pattern control, conjugate the selected whole positive-control list by one $X$ on each zero-valued control, ordering each set of these $X$ gates by wire position. Reverse the ordered middle block by using $XVX$ as its single matrix parameter, not by adding target $X$ occurrences.

Use the selected literal elementary gate list for each call without deleting identity gates or cancelling neighboring gates. In the one-control base use the three target matrices and one control phase as four arbitrary one-qubit gates. Use the same choices and reversed adjoint gate lists for the return swaps. Reuse the supplied clean bit sequentially; each selected clean-bit construction returns it to $0$.

Use the rotation convention of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and define $R_y(\theta):=R_{(0,1,0)}(\theta)$:
$$R_z(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\alpha/2}&0\\0&e^{i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{pmatrix}.$$
For every $U\in U(2)$ there are real $\delta,\alpha,\theta,\beta$ with
$$U=e^{i\delta}R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta).$$
If $\det U=1$, the scalar factor is unnecessary and $U=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta)$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Every $z\ne0$ has a unique representation $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$ with $r=|z|>0$ and $-\pi<\theta\le\pi$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

derivations.claim: By [F2] and [F3], each path swap is an $X$ controlled on the other bits' fixed values, so it exchanges exactly the two indicated basis labels and fixes every other basis vector. Each swap is a permutation of the orthonormal computational basis [F6], hence a unitary. Their chronological product $P$ sends $x=g_0$ to $g_{d-1}$ and fixes $y=g_d$, because the last path edge is deliberately omitted.

For the algorithm's single-control list $S$, direct multiplication of the rotation matrices in [F11] gives $ABC=I$ and $AXBXC=e^{-i\delta}W$. Its two control branches therefore have target blocks $I$ and $e^{-i\delta}W$; the final phase gate makes them $I,W$ exactly, as required by [F9]. The list in [F10] contains exactly two CNOTs and four one-qubit occurrences, even when one is the identity. For the fixed matrix $J$, the orthogonal projectors $(I+X)/2$ and $(I-X)/2$ give $J^2=X$ and unitarity. The list $T(a,b;t)$ restores $b$ and applies target exponent $b-(b\oplus a)+a=2ab$ of $J$, hence is exactly Toffoli. Its cost is $3(2,4)+(2,0)=(8,12)$.

For the ladder $L$ of [F10] with $s\ge3$, each of its two compute/target/uncompute lists restores all spares, since the central $H$ changes only the target. Let $u_j,v_j$ be the values of $a_j$ just before $H$ in the first and second lists. The common initial spare values give $u_1=a_1\oplus c_1c_2$, $v_1=a_1$ and $u_j=a_j\oplus c_{j+1}u_{j-1}$, $v_j=a_j\oplus c_{j+1}v_{j-1}$ for $j\ge2$. Induction yields $u_j\oplus v_j=\prod_{h=1}^{j+1}c_h$, so the two target toggles sum to $c_s(u_{s-2}\oplus v_{s-2})=\prod_{h=1}^s c_h$. Thus $L$ is the exact controlled $X$ and restores its arbitrary spares. Its lists contain $2s-3$ and $2s-5$ Toffolis, giving $E_s=(4s-8)(8,12)$; the CNOT and Toffoli base cases give $E_1,E_2$.

At the level of ideal data gates, let $M$ be the middle operation and $P$ the forward swap permutation. The middle gate acts only on $(g_{d-1},g_d)$; using $XVX$ when the target bit of $g_{d-1}$ is $1$ makes its ordered action exactly $V$. By [F4], the data product is $P^*MP$. Since $P$ sends $(x,y)$ to $(g_{d-1},g_d)$ and no other basis vector into this active pair, the conjugate acts by $V$ on $(x,y)$ and fixes every other data basis vector. Thus the ideal data circuit is the exact two-level unitary, including its scalar phase.

For the balanced list $D$ in [F10], put $a=\prod_{c\in A}c$ and $b=\prod_{c\in B}c$. The ideal actions of $F,G,F,G$ send $z$ to $z\oplus a$ and back and toggle $t$ by $b(z\oplus a)\oplus bz=ab$. Step 2.1 restores the temporary spares after each ladder, so this is valid even when the spares include the other call's controls or target. The inequalities $q+1\ge p-2$ and $p\ge q-1$ ensure enough spares. Two calls of each size have pair $2E_p+2E_{q+1}=B_r$; the one- and two-control cases have pairs $B_1,B_2$. Equality on every basis word extends by [F6] to the full operator $C^r(X)\otimes I_z$, including entangled inputs, so these literal lists meet the borrowed-wire contract of [F8]. All spares are existing wires in each invocation of $D$.

For the no-workspace list $N$, [F12] gives the unitary square root $Z$ prescribed in [F10]: each eigenvalue has modulus one, its half-angle scalar squares to it by the double-angle identities, and that scalar has modulus one. For at least two controls, put $A_0=\prod_{c\in A}c$. The two $D(A;b;t)$ calls restore their borrowed data target exactly by step 3.1. Thus on a basis control branch the target exponent of $Z$ in the five-call list is $b-(b\oplus A_0)+A_0=2A_0b$. Induction on the number of controls, with the one-control case of step 1.2 and the zero-control gate as bases, proves its exact $C^m(W)$ action. No new wire is used. Its literal cost is $Q_{m-1}+2B_{m-1}+2(2,4)$, with $Q_1=(2,4)$ and $Q_0=(0,1)$; the recursion decreases the number of controls and terminates.

In the clean branch, $D(C;w;t)$ computes the controls' AND into $w$, restoring the borrowed data target by step 3.1. The list $S(w,t;W)$ applies $W$ precisely on that branch, and the reversed adjoint $D$ list restores $w=0$ for every data input. Linearity extends this basis calculation to superposed or entangled data. This gives the exact clean-input data operation and pair $2B_m+(2,4)=K_m$ for $m\ge1$; with no controls the sole gate has pair $K_0=Q_0$. No claim about the other initial workspace sector is required.

There are $d-1$ swaps, their $d-1$ inverses, and one controlled-$V$ call. Each zero-valued pattern control is implemented by an $X$ before and after the positive-control call, adding exactly two one-qubit occurrences under [F5]. Steps 4.1–4.2 prove that these selected expansions implement the ideal data gates exactly and each clean-bit call returns its work bit to zero, in the model of [F7]. Sequential composition therefore permits reuse of that bit.

If $d=1$, the swap lists are empty and the single controlled target block acts on $(x,y)$ directly. If $n=1$, there are no controls and the construction is one gate on the sole wire: its matrix is $V$ when $x=0,y=1$, and $XVX$ when $x=1,y=0$, so its action on the selected ordered pair is $V$ in both cases. For the other cases, steps 4.1–4.2 supply the elementary expansions used in step 5.1 with the stated work-bit return, consistently with [F7]. Thus every case is an exact elementary implementation.

A zero control adds two one-qubit $X$ gates, independently of the selected positive-control circuit. The reversed adjoint list has the same pair as its forward list. Adding all forward, reverse, and middle lists therefore gives the claimed total pair. Since $B_r=O(r)$, the recurrence sums to $Q_m=O(m^2)$, whereas $K_m=O(m)$. There are $2d-1$ calls, and at most $m$ negative controls per call, giving the two claimed total bounds for $n\ge2$. Sequential exact clean return permits reuse of one bit even on superposed data. The empty swap lists when $d=1$ and the direct ordered one-qubit block when $n=1$ give the stated boundary cases.

derivations.claim: Normalize $U$ to $U_0=\lambda^{-1}U\in SU(4)$ with $|\lambda|=1$: unitarity and the determinant permutation formula give $|\det U|=1$, so choose $\lambda=e^{i\arg(\det U)/4}$ using [F8]. Put $J=YY$ and $\gamma(W)=WJW^{\mathsf T}J$. For a $2\times2$ matrix $A$, direct multiplication gives $AYA^{\mathsf T}=(\det A)Y$. Therefore local $K=A\otimes B$ with $A,B\in SU(2)$ satisfies $KJK^{\mathsf T}=J$. It follows by substitution and cyclicity of trace that $\operatorname{tr}\gamma(K_1WK_2)=\operatorname{tr}\gamma(W)$ for local $SU(2)$ matrices $K_1,K_2$. This identity uses transpose, not adjoint.

Put $P=ZZ$ and $D(t)=e^{itP}=\cos t\,I+i\sin t\,P$. Since $P$ is diagonal with two $+1$ and two $-1$ entries, $D(t)$ is diagonal unitary with determinant one. Also $JP=PJ$ and $D(t)^{\mathsf T}=D(t)$. Hence $\operatorname{tr}\gamma(D(t)U_0)=\operatorname{tr}(D(t)^2\gamma(U_0))=\cos(2t)\operatorname{tr}\gamma(U_0)+i\sin(2t)\operatorname{tr}(P\gamma(U_0))$. Its imaginary part is $a_0\cos(2t)+b_0\sin(2t)$, with real $a_0=\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{tr}\gamma(U_0)$ and $b_0=\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(P\gamma(U_0))$. If both vanish, take $t=0$. Otherwise choose $\cos(2t)=b_0/(a_0^2+b_0^2)^{1/2}$, $\sin(2t)=-a_0/(a_0^2+b_0^2)^{1/2}$, possible by [F8]. Thus $V=D(t)U_0\in SU(4)$ has real $\operatorname{tr}\gamma(V)$.

Apply [F1] to $V$. The determinant of each local factor and of $N(a,b,c)$ is one: the latter follows from the simultaneous Pauli eigenvalue sign lists $(+,-,+,-)$, $(-,+,+,-)$ and $(+,+,-,-)$ in the Cartan proof, each with sum zero. Thus $e^{4i\delta}=1$ and $e^{2i\delta}\in\{1,-1\}$. The commuting symmetric matrices $XX,YY,ZZ$ commute with $J$, so $\gamma(N)=N^2$. Expand their exponentials using [F2]. Since $XX\,YY\,ZZ=-I$ and all nonconstant products except this triple are traceless, $\operatorname{tr}\gamma(V)=e^{2i\delta}4(\cos(2a)\cos(2b)\cos(2c)+i\sin(2a)\sin(2b)\sin(2c))$. Its imaginary part is zero, so at least one Cartan coordinate is an integer multiple of $\pi/2$.

If, for example, $c=k\pi/2$, its factor is $e^{icZZ}=i^k(ZZ)^k$, a scalar times a product of one-qubit Pauli gates. It commutes with the other Cartan factors and can be absorbed into the exterior local factors. The same applies to $a$ or $b$. Simultaneous conjugation on both qubits by a one-qubit rotation permuting the Pauli axes moves the absent coordinate to $ZZ$. Such permutations are obtained from $R_x(\pi/2),R_y(\pi/2),R_z(\pi/2)$ in [F3]; their conjugations exchange the other two axes up to signs, and each sign is squared in a Pauli product. Thus $V$ is a scalar times exterior local gates and $N(\alpha,\beta,0)$ for real $\alpha,\beta$. All scalar factors are retained as one-qubit scalar gates.

Let $L=R_x(\pi/2)\otimes R_x(\pi/2)$ and let $C$ be [F4]. Its basis action gives $C(X\otimes I)C=XX$ and $C(I\otimes Z)C=ZZ$. Formula [F3] gives $LXXL^*=XX$ and $LZZL^*=YY$ (each rotated $Z$ is $-Y$). Therefore the exact identity $N(\alpha,\beta,0)=LC(R_x(-2\alpha)\otimes R_z(-2\beta))CL^*$ follows by exponentiating the commuting generators. This uses two CNOTs and one-qubit gates only. Combined with step 4.1 it synthesizes $V$ with two CNOTs. Since $V=D(t)\lambda^{-1}U$, the required diagonal is $\Delta=\lambda D(t)^{-1}$ and $U=\Delta V$ exactly. No CNOT is spent implementing $\Delta$ in this factorization assertion.

Write the first two chronological slots as $U_1,S_1,U_2$. By step 5.1, $U_1=\Delta_1V_1$, so the product in [F6] is $U_2S_1\Delta_1V_1$. The separator hypothesis gives $S_1(\Delta_1\otimes I)=(\Delta_1\otimes I)S_1$ branch by branch, even if its $S_{1,x}$ act on several other wires. The product becomes $(U_2\Delta_1)S_1V_1$. The next slot is still an arbitrary unitary on the same two wires. Factor it again and continue. Each of the first $N-1$ slots now uses at most two CNOTs; the final accumulated slot uses at most three by [F5]. All diagonals are absorbed, every separator is unchanged, and no wire is added. For $N=1$ the process performs no migration and uses only the three-CNOT base case. This proves the count $2(N-1)+3$ and exact equality.

derivations.claim: An exact Toffoli has constant cost. Let $V=\frac12((1+i)I+(1-i)X)$. The orthogonal projectors $(I+X)/2,(I-X)/2$ show $V$ is unitary and $V^2=X$. With controls $a,b$, apply chronologically $C_b(V)$ to the target, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{a\to b}$, $C_b(V^*)$, $\mathrm{CNOT}_{a\to b}$, and $C_a(V)$. The bit $b$ returns, and the target exponent is $b-(b\oplus a)+a=2ab$, so its action is $X^{ab}$. By [F1] the three controlled gates and two CNOTs cost at most eight CNOTs and twelve one-qubit gates. No relative phase is discarded.

First construct an $s$-controlled $X$ with $s-2$ borrowed wires, for $s\ge3$. Call the controls $c_1,\ldots,c_s$, the borrowed bits $a_1,\ldots,a_{s-2}$, and the target $t$. Let $T_1$ toggle $a_1$ under $c_1,c_2$; for $2\le j\le s-2$, let $T_j$ toggle $a_j$ under $c_{j+1},a_{j-1}$. Let $Q$ toggle $t$ under $c_s,a_{s-2}$. Apply the list $T_1,\ldots,T_{s-2},Q,T_{s-2},\ldots,T_1$, followed by $T_2,\ldots,T_{s-2},Q,T_{s-2},\ldots,T_2$; for $s=3$ the second list is just $Q$. Each list restores every borrowed bit, since $Q$ changes only $t$ and the compute list is reversed afterward.

Let $u_j,v_j$ be the values of $a_j$ immediately before $Q$ in the first and second lists. Both lists begin with the same borrowed values. We have $u_1=a_1\oplus c_1c_2$, $v_1=a_1$ and, for $j\ge2$, $u_j=a_j\oplus c_{j+1}u_{j-1}$, $v_j=a_j\oplus c_{j+1}v_{j-1}$. Thus $u_j\oplus v_j=\prod_{h=1}^{j+1}c_h$ by induction. The two target toggles add to $c_s(u_{s-2}\oplus v_{s-2})=\prod_{h=1}^s c_h$. Controls and borrowed bits are unchanged. The two lists contain $(2s-3)+(2s-5)=4s-8$ exact Toffolis. For $s=2$ use one Toffoli; for $s=1$ use one CNOT. This auxiliary construction therefore costs $O(s)$ and uses at most $\max\{s-2,0\}$ borrowed wires.

For $r\ge3$, partition the controls into $A,B$ of sizes $p=\lceil r/2\rceil$, $q=\lfloor r/2\rfloor$, and call the extra wire $z$. Put $a=\prod_{j\in A}c_j$, $b=\prod_{j\in B}c_j$. Apply an $A$-controlled $X$ into $z$, a $(B\cup\{z\})$-controlled $X$ into $t$, and repeat these two calls in that order. The first kind can borrow from $B\cup\{t\}$ because $q+1\ge p-2$; the second can borrow from $A$ because $p\ge q-1$. Step 3.1 restores these temporary borrowed wires after each call, for their actual arbitrary values at that call. No wire beyond the original $r+2$ is used.

The four ideal calls send $z$ to $z\oplus a$ and back, while toggling $t$ by $b(z\oplus a)\oplus bz=ab$. Thus their action is precisely $C^r(X)$ with $z$ and every control returned. The two calls of each kind cost $O(p)+O(q+1)=O(r)$. For $r=1,2$, use [F2] or step 1.1 and leave $z$ untouched. Equality on every basis word extends by [F6] to $C^r(X)\otimes I_z$; tensoring with an external identity also proves the entangled-input claim and the return condition [F3].

Let $k\ge0$ controls have computational labels $x\in\{0,1\}^k$, and let $\theta_x\in\mathbb R$. Fix $a\in\{x,y,z\}$. On one target qubit define
$$M=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^k}|x\rangle\langle x|\otimes R_a(\theta_x),\qquad R_a(t)=\exp(-it\sigma_a/2).$$
Then $M$ is exactly synthesized with $2^k$ CNOTs for $k>0$ (the final CNOT restores the parity network). For $a=y,z$ it uses $2^k$ target rotations $R_a(\beta_j)$; for $a=x$ it uses $2^k$ $R_y$ rotations in the fixed target basis described below; for $k=0$ it is one rotation and no CNOT. For $a=x$ and $k>0$ the implementation also uses two fixed target basis-change gates; the $y,z$ implementations need none. One may replace the cyclic Gray traversal by a traversal that omits the final restoration and absorb that final parity into the next block only when that block is explicitly specified.

Use the rotation convention of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and define $R_y(\theta):=R_{(0,1,0)}(\theta)$:
$$R_z(\alpha)=\begin{pmatrix}e^{-i\alpha/2}&0\\0&e^{i\alpha/2}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_y(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta/2)&-\sin(\theta/2)\\\sin(\theta/2)&\cos(\theta/2)\end{pmatrix}.$$
For every $U\in U(2)$ there are real $\delta,\alpha,\theta,\beta$ with
$$U=e^{i\delta}R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta).$$
If $\det U=1$, the scalar factor is unnecessary and $U=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\theta)R_z(\beta)$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $U_0,U_1$ be unitary endomorphisms of $H$. On the control-first direct sum $H\oplus H$, the block unitary $\operatorname{diag}(U_0,U_1)$ factors as
$$\operatorname{diag}(U_0,U_1)=(I\otimes V)\operatorname{diag}(D,D^*)(I\otimes W)$$
for unitary $V,W$ on $H$ and a diagonal unitary $D$ in an orthonormal eigenbasis; $I\otimes V$ denotes $\operatorname{diag}(V,V)$ under $\mathbb C^2\otimes H\cong H\oplus H$.

In the ordered two-qubit basis $|00\rangle,|01\rangle,|10\rangle,|11\rangle$, the controlled-NOT with first wire control and second wire target is

$$\operatorname{CNOT}_{1\to2}|a,t\rangle=|a,t\mathbin{\oplus}a\rangle,\qquad a,t\in\{0,1\}.$$

Equivalently, it is the control block $C(X)=\operatorname{diag}(I,X)$ of [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], where $X$ is the Pauli bit-flip matrix. The wire order is part of the definition.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

Fix a finite gate alphabet $G$ with maximum arity $k:=\max(\{r(g):g\in G\}\cup\{0\})$ and a circuit from [[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]]. The declared **size** is the number of gate occurrences, equivalently $\sum_{t=1}^d|L_t|$; the declared **depth** is the number $d$ of explicit layers, not a minimum over alternate layerings; the **width** is the number $n$ of all wires, including workspace wires. The operation model may also assign weighted gate costs, classical bit costs, and query costs; these are separate coordinates and are summed over the calls actually made.

A workspace wire is an ancilla. A **clean-ancilla promise** specifies computational-basis zero states for the ancillas and requires their exact return for every allowed data input: if $U$ is the implemented unitary, $V_D$ is the declared data unitary, and $|0_A\rangle$ is the specified joint zero vector, then $U(x\otimes|0_A\rangle)=V_Dx\otimes|0_A\rangle$ for every allowed data vector $x$. A **dirty-ancilla promise** permits an arbitrary ancilla state independent of the data input; it may be correlated with an untouched reference. Exact dirty-ancilla restoration means the implemented unitary on data and ancillas is $V_D\otimes I_A$ on the entire joint space, where $V_D$ is the declared unitary on data. The same operator equality then holds after tensoring with the identity on any finite untouched reference. Consequently, product input between the data and the combined ancilla/reference system remains product after the operation. No uncorrelated-output claim is made for an initially data-correlated ancilla.

A controlled or inverse operation is counted only when the operation model explicitly grants that access or supplies a construction; its charge is recorded separately from an ordinary call. Inverse availability and query or gate charges are also recorded separately from controlled forward access. In particular, the matrix of $U$ alone supplies neither a controlled call nor an inverse query, in accordance with [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]] and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]].

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication of [F2] gives $ZR_y(t)Z=R_y(-t)$, with $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$. In the cyclic Gray construction [F1], replace each select-to-target controlled-$X$ by select-to-target controlled-$Z$. On select word $x$, the parity accumulated at mask $p_j$ is now $Z^{p_j\cdot x}$, so conjugation changes the $j$th rotation angle to $(-1)^{p_j\cdot x}\beta_j$. The same Walsh inversion proves the final target angle is $\theta_x$, and the final Gray edge restores the accumulated $Z$ exponent to zero. Thus this network equals $M$ exactly and contains $2^k$ controlled-$Z$ gates. All select bits are unchanged.

Let its final chronological controlled-$Z$ use select wire $r$, and put $Z_r$ for $Z$ on that select wire and identity on the other $k-1$ select wires. In target-first block order this last gate is $E_r=\operatorname{diag}(I_{2^k},Z_r)$. If $T$ is the chronological network with this last gate deleted, [F4] gives the exact identities $M=E_rT$ and $LMR=(LE_r)TR=\operatorname{diag}(L_0,L_1Z_r)\,T\,\operatorname{diag}(R_0,R_1)$. Both $L_0$ and $L_1Z_r$ remain arbitrary $k$-qubit unitaries. This is a block multiplication identity and does not commute $E_r$ through $L$.

Apply [F3] separately to $LE_r$ and $R$. These two generic block-diagonal factors still produce four arbitrary $k$-qubit slots and two diagonal two-block factors. A diagonal factor $\operatorname{diag}(D,D^*)$ is a multiplexed $R_z$ on the first wire: if $D_{xx}=e^{i\alpha_x}$, its two target entries are $e^{i\alpha_x},e^{-i\alpha_x}$ and hence equal $R_z(-2\alpha_x)$. The central $T$ has $2^k-1$ controlled-$Z$ gates. Therefore the rewritten circuit has exactly the required shape and retains the identity in step 2.1.

Set $H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Direct multiplication gives $H^2=I$ and $HXH=Z$, so a controlled-$Z$ on a select-target pair equals $(I\otimes H)\operatorname{CNOT}(I\otimes H)$ in that pair's control-first order. Each costs one CNOT and two one-qubit gates, with no added wire. Thus deleting the terminal $E_r$ saves exactly one CNOT in the central network. Every remaining central gate still acts on the first-wire target or reads other wires only as unchanged selects. The block products in steps 2.1–3.1 are ordinary exact matrix products, so no scalar phase or workspace promise has been suppressed.
